scope.q: What is the typical latency tolerance for acting on a detected fraud pattern before a chargeback is likely to occur?
scope.why: Understanding the required speed of intervention directly impacts architectural choices and the feasibility of human-in-the-loop processes.

scope.q: What specific data sources and features does the fraud team currently use to identify patterns, and what is their current method of 'acting'?
scope.why: This clarifies the existing capabilities and limitations, informing what needs to be automated or augmented, and the required data integration points.

scope.q: What is the acceptable false positive rate for automated fraud interventions, given the potential impact on legitimate customer transactions?
scope.why: This defines the critical trade-off between aggressive fraud prevention and customer experience, directly influencing model design and confidence thresholds.

decomposition.title: Data Ingestion & Feature Engineering
decomposition.why: Fraud detection relies heavily on comprehensive and well-prepared data from various sources, requiring robust ingestion and transformation pipelines.

decomposition.title: Pattern Detection & Anomaly Scoring
decomposition.why: This core component will identify suspicious activities, either through rule-based systems, machine learning models, or a hybrid approach.

decomposition.title: Decision & Action Orchestration
decomposition.why: Once a pattern is detected, there needs to be a system to decide on and execute the appropriate action, which might involve multiple steps or approvals.

decomposition.title: Human-in-the-Loop Review & Workflow
decomposition.why: Complex or high-impact cases will require human oversight and a clear workflow for the fraud team to review, override, or escalate decisions.

decomposition.title: Feedback & Model Retraining Loop
decomposition.why: Fraud patterns evolve, so the system needs to learn from new data and human decisions to continuously improve its detection capabilities.

sprint.title: Setup Data Ingestion MVP
sprint.deliv: Validated ingestion of core transaction data into a raw data store.

sprint.title: Initial Feature Engineering & Storage
sprint.deliv: Basic fraud features (e.g., transaction velocity) computed and stored in feature store.

sprint.title: Rule-Based Detection Engine
sprint.deliv: A simple rule-based engine running, flagging known fraud patterns based on existing team insights.

sprint.title: Basic Action Orchestration & Alerting
sprint.deliv: System can log a detected fraud event and push it to a review queue visible to the fraud team.

sprint.title: Fraud Ops UI for Review
sprint.deliv: Basic web interface for fraud analysts to view flagged transactions and mark them as legitimate/fraudulent.

sprint.title: Automated Action Integration
sprint.deliv: A pre-approved low-risk action (e.g., add internal flag) automatically executed for high-confidence fraud alerts.

sprint.title: Feedback Loop & Monitoring
sprint.deliv: System can record analyst decisions and basic dashboards showing detection rates and false positives.

risks.risk: Lack of high-quality, labeled historical fraud data for model training.
risks.mitigation: Start with a rule-based system augmented by active learning where human analysts label uncertain cases to rapidly generate training data.

risks.risk: False positives leading to legitimate customer friction or lost revenue.
risks.mitigation: Implement a tiered action strategy, starting with low-impact actions for uncertain cases and requiring human review for high-impact interventions. Continuously monitor false positive rates.

risks.risk: Fraud patterns evolving faster than model updates, rendering detection ineffective.
risks.mitigation: Establish a continuous retraining pipeline for models, combined with real-time monitoring of model performance and drift detection. Empower analysts to quickly inject new rules.

risks.risk: Integration complexity with existing legacy payment or customer systems.
risks.mitigation: Prioritize integrations based on data criticality and action impact. Use API gateways and robust error handling; abstract legacy systems behind a modern interface.
